story.title: You are no longer invited to dinner

draft:
The dinner table used to be the unofficial office for ideas, mentorship, and trust‑building.  

Now a growing number of professionals admit they’re “no longer invited to dinner” – not because of etiquette, but because the logistics of hosting have become a silent cost center. Remote work eliminates the commute, but it also erodes the low‑friction moments where senior talent casually mentors juniors over a shared meal.  

I’m seeing two parallel tech trends accelerate this shift: AI‑driven meal‑planning services that outsource the menu to algorithms, and “virtual dinner” platforms that replace the physical plate with a Zoom grid. Both solve convenience but strip away the sensory cues—smell, shared pacing, spontaneous side‑conversations—that make a dinner memorable and, more importantly, a breeding ground for informal collaboration.  

If we want to preserve the relational capital that a dinner once generated, we need to re‑engineer the experience, not just the menu. Perhaps a hybrid model where a few in‑person gatherings are deliberately scheduled around high‑impact project milestones, while the rest remain virtual.  

What small change could you make to bring back the value of a real shared meal in your professional network?
